Waterfront Country Club · Juja

The Ivy Document

How money and stock actually move through the resort — followed from the barrier to the store room, on a live system, with the screens as they really appeared.

Written from a recorded run· 27 August 2026· No screenshot posed

Read this if you work here

This is not a manual for programmers. It follows one guest through one day and shows what the resort's system does at each step, and — just as important — what it refuses to do.

Every screenshot was taken from the system while it was running. Nothing was mocked up, staged, or drawn to look good. Where a screen did not work, this document shows that too, because a picture book of only the working parts is a brochure, not a record.

The one idea worth understanding first

The system never stores what you have. It stores everything that happened, and works out what you have by adding it up.

A cash box does not remember its balance — you count it. This system is the same. Stock is not a number someone types in; it is every delivery in and every sale out, summed. A guest's bill is not a total that gets edited; it is every charge minus every payment.

That sounds like a technical detail. It is the whole reason the numbers can be trusted: there is no field anyone can overwrite. To change what the stock says, you must add a movement — and a movement has a name and a time on it.

ACT 01

The gate

Where cash enters the resort in its rawest form

A guest arrives at the barrier and pays KSh 3,000 to come in. They are handed a numbered wristband. That band is the only thing they need to carry for the rest of the day.

Here is the part that is easy to miss, and it is the cleverest thing in the system: the entry fee is not swallowed by the gate. It becomes credit. The guest has already got their KSh 3,000 back as spending money the moment they walked in. They can drink it, eat it, or spend it at the spa.

One record does both jobs — it settles the physical cash the gate must account for at closing, and it opens the guest's tab at KSh 3,000 in credit. There is no second entry to keep in step, so the two can never disagree.

A small sum worth doing in your head

On the screen above: 20 bands issued today, and entry revenue of KSh 60,000.

Twenty times three thousand is sixty thousand. Those two figures agree because the second one is not stored anywhere — it is worked out from the bands themselves, every time the screen is opened.

Nobody typed 60,000. Nobody can type 60,000. If someone issued a band without taking the money, this number could not quietly stay right.

And read the four bands listed above that total

Bands #18, #19 and #20 each show KSh 1,200 credit left. Band #17 shows KSh 4,200 owed.

Same list, same widget, opposite meanings — and it says which is which in words rather than showing a minus sign and hoping. Gate staff can tell at a glance who still has money on their band and who must settle before leaving.

Band #17 is in that state because it is the band this document tested against: four tilapia dishes were charged to it while proving the stock deduction in Act 3. Which is itself the point — the number moved because something really happened, and it is still moving as the resort is used.

A fault found by trying to photograph a screen

One page could not be captured, and chasing why turned up a real problem.

Asking the station tablet for the band-issue page returns a login screen. Not an error, not "page not found" — a login screen, as though the person had been signed out.

The cause is that the station app has no such page. Issuing a band happens on the gate screen shown above, with the button right there on it. But when the station app is asked for an address it does not recognise, anything it does not recognise, it shows the login screen as a catch-all.

So a mistyped address, a stale bookmark or an old link does not say "that page does not exist." It says, in effect, "sign in again" — sending staff to hunt for a session problem that is not there. It is also exactly how a previous attempt at this document ended up with eight screenshots of a login page filed under eight different dashboard names.

This has since been fixed, and the screen below is the result. An unrecognised address now says so, keeps the person signed in, and offers a way back — which matters on a fixed tablet with no browser buttons to escape with.

Anyone not signed in still goes to the login screen, exactly as before. Both halves are held in place by a test, because repairing one by breaking the other would be worse than the original fault.

Why band numbers cannot repeat

Two guests holding band #14 on the same day would make every bill after that meaningless. So numbers are handed out one at a time: while one is being allocated, every other request waits. The database refuses a duplicate even if the software somehow tried, which means a bug could not create one either.

Numbers restart each day, and the date is part of what makes them unique — so #14 on Monday and #14 on Tuesday are different bands and can never be confused.

The spending ceiling

A band can run to KSh 6,000 — double the entry fee — and no further. At that point staff are told, in plain words, to send the guest back to the gate to add credit.

This is the resort's main protection against walking losses. A guest cannot quietly run up an unlimited tab on a band and disappear; the exposure is capped at a number the owner chose.

ACT 02

One bill, payable anywhere

The band is the account number

The guest swims, orders a beer at the bar, eats at the restaurant, has a massage, takes a boat out. Five departments, five different members of staff, none of whom need to know what the others did.

Every one of those charges lands on the same tab, because the band number is the account number. The guest settles once, at the end, wherever they happen to be.

Nobody adds anything up by hand and nobody stores a running total. The balance is worked out fresh every time it is asked for. That is why the figure the bar sees and the figure the gate sees are always the same figure — there is only one, and it is calculated, not remembered.

The whole idea, in one input box

Above the treatments on the spa screen sits a single field: "Wristband # — charge to band credit."

That is the entire mechanism. The spa attendant does not take money, does not know what the guest spent at the bar, and does not open a bill. They type the band number. The charge joins everything else the guest has done today.

The same field appears at the bar, at the restaurant, at the boat jetty. One number, carried on the guest's wrist, and no cash changing hands in five different places.

The clearest picture in this document

Read the right-hand panel from the bottom up. Payments: CASH −KSh 3,000 — that is the entry fee, sitting on the tab as credit, exactly as Act 1 described. Charges: 1.00× Grilled Tilapia, KSh 1,800. And then Band credit left: KSh 1,200.

Three thousand paid, one thousand eight hundred spent, one thousand two hundred left. The guest can keep spending that anywhere on the property, and there is still only one bill.

Notice what is not there: no running total that someone maintains, no per-department bill to add up at the end, and no way to type over the balance. The 1,200 is the subtraction, performed at the moment you look at it.

The dish is also marked SERVED — the same event that moved 0.35 kg of fish out of the store room in Act 3. One action by the chef, three consequences: the guest is charged, the kitchen ticket clears, and the stock falls.

ACT 03

How the store room knows

The question that has no easy answer at a resort

A bar is easy. Sell a Tusker, remove a Tusker. A kitchen is harder but still manageable — a dish has a recipe, and the recipe says how much of each thing it eats.

The spa is where most systems quietly give up. A massage uses oil. How much? Nobody scans anything. The therapist does not weigh the bottle. And a boat ride burns fuel that no till ever sees.

This system answers it by refusing to guess. Every sellable thing must be one of exactly four kinds, and a thing nobody has classified cannot be sold at all.

Read the badges on that screenshot

Jet Ski Ride is a RECIPE — it burns fuel, so selling one deducts fuel. It also shows 50% cost, meaning half of the KSh 3,500 goes on what it consumes.

Kayaking, the pool day pass, hiking and the cycling tour are SERVICE — somebody confirmed these genuinely consume nothing.

Boat Ride, Fishing Trip and Golf Cart Ride are in red: NOT TRACKED — CANNOT SELL. All three burn fuel and nobody has said how much yet, so the system will not sell them.

That is the enforcement, printed on the row. Not a warning to be ignored — the item is simply unavailable until a human decides. The grey "Consumes nothing" button beside each one is the one-tap way to settle it, for the cases where that is the true answer.

Why the last box matters most

The difference between SERVICE and UNTRACKED is the difference between "a person checked, and this genuinely uses nothing" and "nobody has looked at this yet."

They would both deduct zero. Most systems treat them the same and silently leak stock forever. Here they are separate on purpose, and that separation is what makes it safe to block the sale — the system is not refusing because it is broken, it is refusing because a decision is genuinely missing.

The bug this document exists partly to record

Until recently, the spa leaked completely — and so did water sports, and every other department that hands something over immediately.

The reason was subtle. Stock was deducted at the moment the kitchen or bar marked an order ready. But a massage is never marked ready by anyone; it goes straight to served. So the deduction step was never reached, and the safety net that was supposed to warn about missing recipes sat behind the same door.

Everything that did not pass through a kitchen pass or a bar counter consumed nothing at all, and no warning was ever raised. It is fixed, and the figures below are from a run that proves it.

Watching it happen, once, on purpose

Claims like the ones above are cheap. So here is one sale, put through the running system while this document was being written, with the store room watched on either side of it.

The dish was a Grilled Tilapia at KSh 1,800. Its recipe says one portion takes 0.35 kg of tilapia fillet, along with oil, spices, onions and tomatoes.

StepWhat the system didTilapia fillet in store
Before—7.2000 kg
Waiter takes the orderOrder created on band #17's tab7.2000 kg
Order sentTicket appears on the kitchen queue7.2000 kg
Chef marks it readyIngredients deducted automatically6.8500 kg
The number that matters

7.2000 − 6.8500 = 0.3500 kg. Exactly the recipe line. Not approximately.

Nobody in the kitchen typed a stock figure. The chef marked a dish ready, which is the one thing a chef was going to do anyway, and the store room updated itself.

The deduction is also stamped with who — the ledger row reads Auto-consumption: order_item=… against the chef's name. So a variance at the end of the month can be walked back to individual dishes.

Where the stock actually lives

Ingredients belong to departments, which is why a bar manager cannot see or spend kitchen stock. The current spread across the resort:

DepartmentSellable itemsIngredients held
Kitchen010
Restaurant110
Bar58
Water Activities84
Spa & Gym54
Housekeeping04
Grounds03

Restaurant sells eleven dishes and holds no ingredients of its own — it cooks from the kitchen's store. That split is deliberate: the people who sell are not the people who hold the stock, which is the oldest control in hospitality.

ACT 04

The guest leaves, the day closes

Where a system either catches a shortfall or hides it

At the barrier, the band is closed. Any credit the guest did not spend is forfeited — it becomes resort revenue. There is no refund path in the system, and that is a decision, not an omission: a refund at the gate is cash leaving the building at the least supervised moment of the day.

Bands that were never closed — the guest wandered out, staff got busy — are swept at end of day and forfeited together, so nothing stays open overnight quietly holding credit.

Counting the cash drawer

At the end of a shift the system already knows what should be in the drawer — it is the sum of every cash payment taken. Staff count what is actually there and enter it.

If the two disagree, the difference is recorded as a shortfall against the person who counted. It is not smoothed over and there is no button to make it balance.

Worth saying out loud before you go live

This strictness is correct, and it will hurt in week one. New staff make counting mistakes, and every one of them will be recorded against a real person's name.

Decide in advance what a first-week shortfall means, and tell staff before their first shift — not after their first mistake.

ACT 05

Every dashboard, and the question it answers

A screen that answers no question is a screen nobody opens

There are three separate apps, and which one a person gets is decided by their job, not by a setting they can change. A waiter cannot reach the owner's app by typing a different address — the system checks who they are on every single request, not just when they log in.

That last point matters more than it sounds. If a person is dismissed at 2pm, their access dies at 2pm, even if their phone still has them logged in.

AppWho carries itRuns on
StationTills, the gate, the kitchen pass, the spa deskFixed tablets on resort wifi
EmployeeEvery member of staff, and managersTheir own phone
OwnerThe owner, and the manager for some screensPhone or laptop, from anywhere

Twelve screens. Each one exists to answer a question the owner would otherwise have to ask a person.

The audit screen deserves a paragraph

Every action writes a line, and each line carries a fingerprint of the line before it. Remove or edit any entry and every fingerprint after it stops matching.

You cannot quietly delete an inconvenient row. You can only add. That is what makes the answer to "who voided that order at 9pm?" worth having.

The captured screen holds 1,510 entries and reads like a diary of the day: ivan.kipchoge order.send, hassan.omondi gate.issue_band band=17, three clock-ins with the tablet's address, a login.

Follow that band number across this document. Here in the audit log, band=17 is recorded as issued by hassan.omondi. On the gate screen in Act 1, band #17 appears again in the recent list, now showing KSh 4,200 owed after the tilapia charged to it.

Two screens, written by different parts of the system, describing the same wristband at two moments in its life. Nobody linked them. They agree because neither is storing its own copy of the truth.

The manager's screens

The manager runs the day. These screens sit inside the staff app, and open only for people at manager level or above.

ScreenThe question it answers
Manager homeWhat needs me right now?
CashDoes the drawer match what the system says was taken?
StaffWho is on the books, and what is each person allowed to do?
AttendanceWho actually turned up, and when?
Shifts & rosterWho is meant to be working, and is anyone double-booked?
LeaveWho has asked for time off, and can the roster take it?
PurchasesWhat has been requested, and what has it cost against budget?
MenuWhat is on sale, at what price, and what does it cost to make?
Front deskDeposits, confirmations and check-ins waiting to be dealt with.
Who is allowed to set a price

The head chef owns recipes, ingredients, dishes and their prices — for the kitchen and the bar, because a cocktail is a recipe like any other.

The manager owns the service catalogue and prices across every department — the spa treatments, the boat rides, the day passes.

These do not overlap, and the boundary is enforced. A chef cannot reclassify a spa treatment as a kitchen item in order to take control of it.

What ordinary staff see

Four screens, deliberately. A waiter does not need a dashboard; they need to clock in, see their shifts, read what they have been sent, and know how they are doing.

Follow the fish one last time

That inbox reads: "Order ready — Band #20. 1.00× Grilled Tilapia is ready for pickup." And again for bands #19, #18 and #17.

Those are the same tilapia dishes that appear on band #20's bill in Act 2, that moved 0.35 kg of fish out of the store room in Act 3, and that left band #17 owing KSh 4,200 on the gate screen in Act 1.

One chef tapping "ready" charged a guest, cleared a kitchen ticket, deducted stock, wrote an audit line, and told the waiter to collect — and every screen in this document is looking at that single event from a different chair.

Two doors, not one

Look at the menu down the left of that screenshot: Clock, Alerts, Profile, Calendar, Incident. That is everything this waiter can reach. There is no Schedule, no Manager, no Finance — the menu shows only what the person can actually use.

The screenshot itself is the second door. It is what happens if someone types the address anyway, or follows an old bookmark. The menu hides it; the guard refuses it.

And it says so plainly — "You don't have permission to view this page" with a way back. An earlier version showed a blank page or told people to check their internet connection, which sent staff chasing a network fault that did not exist.

A bug worth remembering from the clock screen

For a period, the "Clock Out" button clocked people in. The button knew what it was called but the request underneath it was hard-wired the wrong way.

Nobody could end a shift, and because pay is worked out from these records, it was a payroll problem rather than a cosmetic one. It is fixed — the direction is now decided once, when the button is tapped, and carried through.

The station tablets

These are the fixed screens on the resort floor — the gate, the bar, the kitchen pass, the spa desk, the front desk. They hold the fewest screens of the three apps on purpose.

The station app is not allowed to reach the finance screens at all. Not hidden from them — unable to reach them. A till on a public counter is the easiest device in the resort to walk up to, so it carries the least.

ACT 06

What is real, and what is waiting

The part most documents like this leave out

Everything above works. But a system that works and a system that is ready are different things, and the gap is not code — it is information only the resort has.

The menu is mostly undecided

Of 29 sellable items, only 13 have been classified. The other 16 are still UNTRACKED, which means the system will refuse to sell them.

KindCountMeaning
RECIPE5Deducts each ingredient in its recipe
DIRECT2Deducts one of itself — a bottle, a can
SERVICE6Someone confirmed it consumes nothing
UNTRACKED16Nobody has decided yet — cannot be sold

This is not a fault to be fixed by a programmer. It is roughly an hour of decisions that only the head chef and the manager can make: how much fuel a boat trip burns, how much oil a massage uses, what goes into each dish.

Almost nothing has a cost yet

There are 33 ingredients on the system and exactly 1 of them knows what it costs — because exactly 1 purchase has ever been recorded.

Cost is not typed in; it is worked out from what was actually paid for deliveries. That is the right design — nobody can inflate a cost to hide a margin — but it means the profit screens stay blank until real purchases go in. Record a few weeks of deliveries and the entire menu-profit picture lights up on its own.

Why the screens say "cannot be measured" instead of guessing

A dish with no ingredient costs could be shown with an assumed margin. It would look better and it would be a lie — and someone would eventually drop a profitable dish because of it.

The system says it does not know. That is a feature, and it is the same instinct behind refusing to sell an unclassified item.

Three things deliberately not built

Not builtWhy not
Tax invoices (eTIMS) A tax invoice needs a serial number and identifiers issued once that must never change. The format is the accountant's decision. Choosing one now and changing it later would mean reissuing every invoice already handed to a guest.
Offline tills If two tablets take an order for the same table while the network is down, one of them has to lose. Who wins, and what the waiter sees, are decisions about how the floor runs — not something to guess at. Built on a guess, it would look like it worked and quietly lose orders.
Spoilage sensitivity The alert currently treats 10 litres of milk the same as 10 grams of saffron. Fixing it properly needs real volume history, which arrives with the purchase records above.

VAT is built, but unconfirmed

Prices are treated as including 16% VAT, which is the Kenyan hospitality norm. The rate is stored as a setting rather than written into the software, so it can be changed when the law changes without anyone touching code — and each sale keeps a copy of the rate that applied on the day.

That last detail matters: when the rate changes, last year's receipts must still show last year's rate. They do.

What remains is a question for the accountant, not the system: are these prices really VAT-inclusive, and which items are exempt or zero-rated?

METHOD

How this document was made

So you can judge whether to believe it

Every screenshot here came from the system running on a real machine, driven automatically, one screen at a time. Nothing was drawn or arranged.

There was an earlier attempt at this. It produced forty screenshots, and eight of them were the same image — the login screen — saved under eight different names: "manager cash", "manager menu", "manager staff", and five more. That run had navigated without ever logging in, and photographed whatever happened to be on the screen.

The rule that came out of it

The capture used for this document proves it is on the right screen before it takes the picture. If it cannot find something that belongs to that screen, it records a failure and moves on.

A missing screenshot is honest. A wrong screenshot with a confident caption is worse than nothing, because it is the kind of mistake nobody catches by reading.

The capture runCount
Screens attempted41
Verified and photographed39
Distinct images (no screen photographed twice)39
Reported as failures on the first pass7
Still genuinely uncaptured after checking2

What those seven "failures" turned out to be

This is the interesting part, and it is the same lesson twice over: the tool doing the measuring is often the thing that is wrong.

Reported as failedWhat it actually was
Manager home
and Clock		 Fine. The capture was looking for wording that does not appear on those screens. Photographed successfully on a second pass and both are in this document.
Schedule, Performance, Stock count Working exactly as designed. All three are manager-level screens, and the accounts used were a waiter and the head chef. They showed "Access restricted" — the correct answer, not a fault.
Band issue A real fault, and the best thing this exercise found. The station app has no such page, and answers any address it does not recognise with a login screen instead of "page not found" — see Act 1.
Tab detail Slow to appear on the first attempt; captured on a later one. It is in this document.
Two screenshots came out identical, and one was deleted

"Schedule" and "Performance" produced byte-for-byte the same picture — because for a waiter they genuinely are the same screen: the access-restricted notice.

That is honest, but captioning one image as two different screens is exactly the mistake this document was written to avoid. One was deleted. It appears once, labelled as what it is.

The stock deduction was not taken on trust either

The capture recorded stock before and after but never actually sold anything in between, so both readings were identical — which proves nothing in either direction.

So one Grilled Tilapia was put through the live system by hand: ordered, sent, and marked ready by the head chef. The tilapia fillet fell from 7.2000 kg to 6.8500 kg. That is 0.3500 kg — the recipe line exactly. Those are the figures in Act 3, and they were produced that way.

Found along the way

Photographing a system turns out to be a decent way of testing it. Three things surfaced that no test had asked about:

FindingWhy it mattersWeight
The station tablets answered any unknown address with a login screen A typo or an old bookmark looked like being signed out, sending staff after a problem that was not there. It is also how a previous run produced eight login screens filed as eight dashboards. Now says "Page not found", keeps you signed in, and offers a way back — with a test holding both that and the signed-out case in place. Fixed
The notifications screen had no title Every other screen names itself. This one opened straight into a list, so there was nothing to orient a new member of staff — and nothing on the page to identify it in a screenshot. It now names itself and shows the unread count. Fixed
The station's "Access restricted" screen was a dead end Found while fixing the above: it offered no way back. On a wall-mounted tablet with no browser buttons, the only escape was signing out. The staff app had already been fixed; the tablets had not. Fixed
Staff land on the screen they need, by department Not a fault — a good detail worth knowing. Kitchen staff open the kitchen queue, bar staff the bar, gate staff the gate. Nobody is asked to navigate to their own job. Working
This document has already been corrected once

The first published version explained the missing band-issue screenshot as a security measure — that staff must enter a PIN to start a shift before they can hand out wristbands. It read well and it was wrong.

There is no such rule. The page simply does not exist on that tablet, and the login screen is what the app shows for anything it does not recognise. The invented explanation was more flattering than the truth, which is exactly why it needed checking.

Corrected here rather than quietly edited out, because a document about not trusting confident captions should show its own.

The same principle applies to the numbers. Anything shown in this style was read from the running system, not written from memory.

The Ivy Document — Waterfront Country Club, Juja.

Written 27 August 2026 from a recorded run of the live system. Where this document and the system disagree, the system is right and this document is out of date.
